hook: Release 40 pill bugs into a chamber with a moist side and a dry side, and 29 end up on the moist side. A preference, or just luck? Flip 40 coins and you rarely get exactly 20 heads. The chi-square test measures how far your counts are from what "no preference" predicts and tells you whether that gap is too big for chance.

options: the independent variable has no effect; differences are due to chance
the independent variable causes the predicted effect
the experiment has no control group
prereq.why: The null is the "no effect" statement that the test tries to reject.

prereq.q: Data lead you to fail to reject a null hypothesis. What does that mean?
options: The data did not show an effect
The data proved there is no effect
prereq.why: Failing to reject means the evidence is not strong enough; it never proves the null.

figure.caption: A complete chi-square test on the pill bug data: expected counts, χ² = 8.1, df = 1, critical value 3.84, reject the null.

chain.cause: The null hypothesis predicts how the total should split among categories (no preference: 20 and 20).
chain.effect: That prediction gives an expected count, e, for each category.

chain.cause: Observed counts, o, differ from expected; squaring the differences and dividing by e scales each gap to the size of the category.
chain.effect: Adding the terms gives χ² = Σ (o − e)² ÷ e: 4.05 + 4.05 = 8.1.

chain.cause: More categories give more chances for chance gaps to add up.
chain.effect: You look up the critical value for df = categories − 1 (here 1) at p = 0.05: 3.84.

chain.cause: χ² (8.1) is greater than the critical value (3.84).
chain.effect: A gap this large would happen less than 5% of the time if the null were true (p < 0.05), so you reject the null hypothesis.

chain.cause: If χ² had been below the critical value…
chain.effect: …you would fail to reject the null: the counts would fit "no preference" well enough to be chance.

ideas: Worked example. o = 29 moist, 11 dry; e = 20, 20. χ² = (29 − 20)² ÷ 20 + (11 − 20)² ÷ 20 = 4.05 + 4.05 = 8.1. df = 1; critical value (p = 0.05) = 3.84. 8.1 > 3.84: reject the null.
Formula sheet: χ² = Σ (o − e)² ÷ e, with df = number of categories − 1. Use the p = 0.05 column unless told otherwise.
Bigger χ² means a worse fit to the null. χ² greater than the critical value means p is less than 0.05: reject. Otherwise, fail to reject.
Always use counts, never percentages or means: chi-square depends on how many individuals were counted.

misconception.wrong: A large chi-square value means the data support the null hypothesis.
misconception.right: A large χ² means observed counts are far from what the null predicts. Above the critical value, you reject the null; a small χ² is what fits the null.

summary: The chi-square test compares observed counts with the counts expected under a null hypothesis: χ² = Σ (o − e)² ÷ e. Degrees of freedom are categories − 1. If χ² is greater than the critical value at p = 0.05, the deviation is unlikely to be chance and the null is rejected; otherwise you fail to reject it. Use counts, not percentages, and never "prove" or "accept" a hypothesis.
